passage.bullet: Safe central bend on the River Tigris → helped Caliph al-Mansur rule wide Abbasid lands
Deep canals linked the Tigris and Euphrates → fresh water grew lush dates and wheat
Reed quffa boats met Silk Road caravans → turned Baghdad into a busy trading crossroads

context.bullet: Surrounding desert lands were dry and hot → great cities needed reliable year-round river water
Heavy goods moved slowly overland → wide rivers carried food and timber far faster

stems.stem: Caliph al-Mansur chose the Tigris because deep ____________ linked it to the ____________, watering crops like ____________.
Round woven ____________ boats and overland ____________ caravans met there, bringing rich ____________ and spices.
Positioned at a ____________ bend in the empire, this fertile river site helped the ____________ govern wide lands.

lesson_1.watch_out: Baghdad was not built in dry empty desert—canals between the Tigris and Euphrates made its soil rich and green.

passage.bullet: Architects lit cotton seeds in a two-kilometre circle → mapped out a bold round city
100,000 builders baked millions of mud bricks → raised thick double walls and a moat
Four iron gates and straight streets → pointed inward to the Great Mosque and palace

context.bullet: Tigris riverbanks had scarce stone → builders shaped abundant river mud into tough sun-baked bricks
Each gate faced a major province like Khorasan or Syria → linked Baghdad across the empire

stems.stem: After architects traced a ____________ circle in flaming cotton seeds, ____________ workers built thick ____________ and a moat.
Four guarded ____________ pierced the outer ring, with straight ____________ leading towards the city heart.
Named Madinat al-Salam, meaning ____________, the centre held the ____________ beside the Green Dome Palace.

lesson_1.watch_out: Baghdad did not grow by accident—architects planned its exact two-kilometre circle before laying a single mud brick.

passage.bullet: Nearly one million people lived in Baghdad → dwarfed London or Winchester at 10,000 residents
Paved streets, canals, bathhouses, and libraries → made Baghdad far grander than muddy village lanes
Most Anglo-Saxon families lived in smoky thatched timber huts → contrasted with brick-built Baghdad

context.bullet: Booming river and caravan trade → pushed markets and gardens far outside the original Round City
Old Roman stone towns in Britain had shrunk → most Anglo-Saxons farmed in small villages

stems.stem: By AD 900, bustling Baghdad held nearly ____________ people, whereas London or Winchester held only ____________.
While Baghdad’s citizens enjoyed ____________ streets, bathhouses, and ____________, Anglo-Saxon lanes remained ____________.
Most families in Anglo-Saxon Britain lived in smoky ____________ huts with ____________ roofs rather than brick city districts.

lesson_1.watch_out: Anglo-Saxon Britain was not completely empty of towns, but even London was around one hundred times smaller than Baghdad.

passage.bullet: Watermills pulped old cotton and linen rags → produced smooth paper cheaply and quickly
Rag paper replaced animal parchment → saved the huge cost of scraping whole calfskin herds
Over 100 shops filled the Paper Sellers’ Market → spread affordable poetry and star charts

context.bullet: Baghdad’s central Silk Road routes → carried Chinese craft secrets west through Samarkand
Fast river canals around Baghdad → drove heavy mill hammers to pulp rags at scale

stems.stem: Using Chinese methods learned via Samarkand, watermills beat ____________ and ____________ rags into cheap, smooth paper.
Unlike European scribes who scraped costly ____________, Baghdad’s bookmakers could copy texts ____________ and affordably.
Affordable paper fuelled over ____________ shops in the ____________, selling star charts and poetry.

lesson_2.watch_out: Baghdad’s craftworkers did not invent paper from scratch—they adopted Chinese paper-making via Samarkand and scaled it up with watermills.

passage.bullet: Al-Ma’mun bought fragile Greek, Persian, and Sanskrit scrolls → saved crumbling books from vanishing
Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators like Hunayn ibn Ishaq → put world texts into Arabic
Scholars tested ancient claims instead of copying blindly → corrected old scientific mistakes

context.bullet: Abundant rag paper from Baghdad’s mills → let scribes copy rescued texts many times over
One million citizens from varied backgrounds → brought fluency in many ancient languages together

stems.stem: Messengers gathered fragile scrolls from ____________, Persia, and ____________ before their pages crumbled away.
Inside the House of Wisdom, Muslim, ____________, and ____________ thinkers such as ____________ translated texts into Arabic.
Rather than copying ancient writers ____________, Baghdad’s thinkers ____________ every claim and fixed errors.

lesson_2.watch_out: House of Wisdom translators were not just copyists—they actively questioned, tested, and corrected errors in ancient Greek books.

passage.bullet: Fatima al-Fihri funded al-Qarawiyyin in Fez in AD 859 → built an enduring mosque college
Students gathered at al-Qarawiyyin for maths, star maps, and law → continues teaching today
Queen Zubayda paid masons for stone wells and pools → saved pilgrims walking to Mecca

context.bullet: Islamic teachings praised lasting public charity → inspired wealthy women patrons to fund schools and water
Crossing scorching Arabian sands on foot → made reliable stone reservoirs a life-or-death lifeline

stems.stem: In AD 859, Fatima al-Fihri used her wealth in ____________ to found ____________ for studying law and maths.
Along the hot desert road to ____________, Queen Zubayda funded stone ____________ and pools to save travellers.
Both visionary women acted as generous ____________ whose public works shaped ____________ and travel for centuries.

lesson_2.watch_out: Do not assume only male caliphs funded Golden Age projects—wealthy women like Fatima al-Fihri and Zubayda built major colleges and water networks.

passage.bullet: Al-Khwarizmi spread digits 0 to 9 and al-Jabr → made sums easier and founded algebra
Craftworkers like Mariam al-Asturlabi built brass astrolabes → helped travellers navigate and find Mecca
Al-Jazari engineered his Elephant Water Clock with hidden floats → chimed every half hour accurately

context.bullet: Translators had studied Sanskrit number scrolls → helped Baghdad mathematicians build on Indian zero
European scribes still used Roman letters like MMDCC → lacked zero for quick place-value sums

stems.stem: Championing Hindu-Arabic numerals including ____________, scholar ____________ wrote a book that gave us ____________.
Skilled makers such as ____________ crafted brass astrolabes so sailors and travellers could check ____________ and find ____________.
Using hidden water floats, engineer ____________ built the ____________ to mark each half hour with cymbals.

lesson_3.watch_out: Digits 0 to 9 originated in India, not Arabia alone—Baghdad scholars like al-Khwarizmi adopted, refined, and spread Hindu-Arabic numerals.

passage.bullet: Built a pinhole camera obscura in a dark room → disproved ancient Greek eye-ray claims
Proved light travels in straight lines into our eyes → laid foundations for modern cameras
Bimaristans gave free clean wards, medicines, and recovery money → treated rich and poor alike

context.bullet: House of Wisdom scholars questioned translated Greek writers → inspired hands-on experiments over blind trust
Early medieval European care mostly offered monastery prayer → lacked Baghdad’s free secular teaching wards

stems.stem: Inside a dark pinhole ____________, Ibn al-Haytham proved that light travels in ____________ into our ____________.
Free teaching hospitals welcoming rich and ____________ patients featured clean wards, fountains, and a stocked ____________.
When patients left to rest at home, bimaristans even gave them clean ____________ and ____________.

lesson_3.watch_out: Ancient Greeks thought rays shot out from human eyes—Ibn al-Haytham proved the exact opposite, showing light enters our eyes in straight lines.

passage.bullet: Al-Razi hung fresh meat across Baghdad → built the hospital where clean air slowed rotting
Detailed patient records and nourishing nursing meals → helped al-Razi separate measles from smallpox
Al-Zahrawi drew 200 surgical instruments and used catgut stitches → dissolved safely inside healing wounds

context.bullet: Cheap rag paper and clear ink diagrams → spread al-Zahrawi’s tool drawings to doctors everywhere
Busy bimaristan wards gathered many patients → let doctors compare rashes and fevers side by side

stems.stem: After hanging ____________ across town to find clean air, al-Razi kept bedside notes separating ____________ from ____________.
Working in Spain around AD 1000, surgeon al-Zahrawi drew over ____________ tools such as ____________ and bone saws.
Using natural ____________ thread, al-Zahrawi closed deep cuts with stitches that ____________ safely inside the body.

lesson_3.watch_out: Al-Razi did not hang meat around Baghdad as magic—it was a practical test to find the cleanest, freshest air for patients.

passage.bullet: Two-humped camel caravans trekked Silk Road trails → carried Chinese silk, porcelain, and Indian spices
Walled caravanserais stood every thirty kilometres → locked brick gates shielded merchants from night bandits
Courtyard wells and warm meals refreshed tired caravans → kept goods flowing into Baghdad’s souks

context.bullet: Baghdad’s central spot between Asia, Africa, and Europe → drew luxury goods from three continents
Thirty kilometres matched one full day’s camel march → ensured nobody camped unprotected in open desert

stems.stem: Long trains of two-humped ____________ crossed Silk Road trails carrying goods like ____________, porcelain, and pepper.
Spaced every ____________ kilometres, fortified inns called ____________ locked their brick gates against desert ____________.
Rested by cool ____________ water each night, merchants safely reached Baghdad’s shaded ____________ to sell their wares.

lesson_4.watch_out: Merchants rarely walked the entire Silk Road alone—spaced caravanserais every thirty kilometres made dangerous desert journeys safe and regular.

passage.bullet: Coconut-stitched wooden dhows with triangular sails → rode Indian Ocean winds from Basra to China
Captains measured star heights with brass astrolabes → guided cargo ships safely across open seas
Bankers wrote signed paper sakk slips → let merchants cash money afar without pirate risks

context.bullet: River boats sailed straight down the Tigris to Basra → connected Baghdad to ocean shipping
Baghdad’s rag paper mills and star astrolabes → directly powered safer banking and sea voyages

stems.stem: Sailing south through ____________, wooden dhows stitched with ____________ rope caught winds towards ____________ and China.
At night on the open Indian Ocean, captains steered accurately by checking stars with brass ____________.
Instead of risking heavy ____________ sacks to pirates, traders carried signed paper sakk slips that gave us the word ____________.

lesson_4.watch_out: A sakk was not paper banknotes like modern cash—it was a signed banker’s promise that gave English our word cheque.

passage.bullet: Hoards of Abbasid silver dirhams buried near Jorvik → prove Islamic coins reached Viking York
Vikings traded furs and swords up Russian rivers → earned pure Arabic-script silver coins
King Offa of Mercia minted an AD 774 gold coin → copied an Abbasid Arabic dinar

context.bullet: Abbasid mints kept silver purity remarkably high → northern traders trusted dirhams by weight everywhere
Small Anglo-Saxon kingdoms still linked into wide trade → valued prestigious gold designs from afar

stems.stem: Flowing north along ____________ rivers, pure Abbasid silver ____________ were prized by Vikings and buried near Jorvik.
Around AD 774, Mercian ruler ____________ struck a famous gold coin copying an Islamic ____________.
Swirling ____________ letters stamped onto coins found in Britain prove that Islamic ____________ networks stretched across Europe.

lesson_4.watch_out: King Offa of Mercia did not convert to Islam—he copied an Abbasid gold dinar because Islamic coins were widely trusted in international trade.

passage.bullet: Thick brick walls enclosed shaded courtyards with fountains → shielded rooms from blazing Iraq sun
Tall badgir windcatchers scooped breezes down indoors → pushed rising hot air out naturally
Neighbourhood hammams offered tiled washrooms, olive-oil soap, and rosewater → kept citizens clean before prayers

context.bullet: Baghdad’s canal network supplied running water → fed courtyard fountains and dozens of neighbourhood bathhouses
Regular washing before daily prayers and meals → reduced sickness compared with smoky unwashed huts

stems.stem: Thick brick walls surrounded shaded ____________ where splashing ____________ and orange trees cooled the air.
Rising above rooftops, tall towers called ____________ scooped fresh breezes indoors and pushed ____________ air out.
Before daily ____________ and meals, residents visited tiled hammams where they scrubbed with ____________ soap and splashed ____________.

lesson_5.watch_out: Badgir windcatchers used zero electricity or fans—clever tower angles captured natural breezes to cool rooms in blazing desert heat.

passage.bullet: Waterwheel orchards grew lemons, oranges, aubergines, spinach, and pomegranates → enriched everyday Baghdad diets
Cooks simmered spiced stews with almonds and cane sugar → served on shiny lustreware bowls
Tilers crafted geometric stars, arabesque vines, and Qur’an calligraphy → honoured God without statues

context.bullet: Caravans and dhows brought citrus and sugar from Asia → farmers adapted them along Tigris canals
Mastery of geometry and brass compasses → helped artists tile repeating star patterns without gaps

stems.stem: Watered by canals, farmers grew ____________, oranges, and ____________, while cooks sweetened spiced stews with ____________.
Families served warm meals inside metallic-glazed ____________ bowls made by skilled Baghdad potters.
Avoiding human or animal statues, mosque tilers combined ____________ star patterns, curling ____________ vines, and sacred ____________.

lesson_5.watch_out: Mosque artists did not avoid statues because they lacked skill—Islamic worship avoided human figures to honour God alone.

passage.bullet: Royal looms wove bright silk robes with tiraz bands → displayed embroidered Arabic inscriptions
Master glassblowers gilded enamelled glass lamps → lit mosques and rooms with glowing verses
Families sipped fruit syrups on carpets playing shatranj → gave the world chess and checkmate

context.bullet: Silk Road trade brought raw silk thread into Baghdad → supplied royal weaving workshops
Cultural links with India and Persia → brought early strategy board games into Abbasid courtyards

stems.stem: Royal workshops wove bright ____________ robes decorated with embroidered Arabic bands known as ____________.
Skilled glassblowers crafted gilded, enamelled ____________ inscribed with sacred verses to brighten indoor spaces.
Sitting on woven carpets, families sipped fruit syrups and played ____________, crying Shah mat for ____________.

lesson_5.watch_out: Checkmate does not mean checking a friend—it comes from the Persian-Arabic shatranj phrase Shah mat, meaning the king is helpless.

passage.bullet: Abbasid lands split into rival kingdoms with a weak army → left borders poorly defended
Hulagu Khan’s vast Mongol cavalry surrounded both Tigris banks → trapped Baghdad without escape
Wooden trebuchets smashed Baghdad’s brick walls → Mongol troops burned the House of Wisdom

context.bullet: Al-Mansur’s mud-brick walls had guarded Baghdad for centuries → crumbled under heavy boulder bombardments
Siege destruction wrecked ancient Tigris irrigation canals → crippled surrounding farmland after AD 1258

stems.stem: After the Abbasid Empire split into ____________ kingdoms, Baghdad’s small ____________ could no longer guard its borders.
Surrounding both banks of the ____________, Mongol engineers built giant wooden ____________ to smash the brick walls.
Once troops stormed inside in February 1258, fires destroyed palaces, canals, and the famous ____________.

lesson_6.watch_out: Baghdad did not fall simply because Mongols rode fast horses—Abbasid political division and heavy wooden trebuchets broke the city’s defences.

passage.bullet: Duplicate paper books sat safely in Cairo, Damascus, and Samarkand → survived Baghdad’s burning
Seventy libraries in Al-Andalus Córdoba → preserved Arabic science far beyond Mongol reach
Muslim, Jewish, and Christian translators in Toledo turned Arabic books into Latin → sparked Europe’s Renaissance

context.bullet: Cheap rag paper had produced thousands of copies → stopped one fire erasing all learning
Baghdad once translated Greek into Arabic → Toledo now passed enriched Arabic science into Latin

stems.stem: Golden Age learning survived 1258 because ____________ copies were stored safely in Damascus, ____________, and Cairo.
Far west in Islamic Spain, called ____________, the city of Córdoba held ____________ libraries filled with books.
Multi-faith translators in Toledo turned works by ____________ and Ibn Sina into ____________ for European readers.

lesson_6.watch_out: Golden Age science was not lost forever in 1258—cheap paper had already spread duplicate books to libraries from Cairo to Spain.

passage.bullet: Digits 0 to 9, algebra, and algorithms → power school sums and modern smartphones
Ibn al-Haytham’s optics and clean bimaristan wards → shaped cameras, glasses, and modern hospitals
Arabic trade and science gave English words like zero, sugar, lemon, sofa, and cotton

context.bullet: Latin translations from Spain entered European universities → carried Baghdad’s discoveries into modern classrooms
Mud-brick walls fell to Hulagu Khan in 1258 → shared human knowledge outlived any empire

stems.stem: Whenever we write digits ____________, solve ____________, or run a phone ____________, we use Baghdad’s maths.
Smartphone ____________ and glasses build on Ibn al-Haytham’s light proofs, while ____________ echo clean bimaristans.
Everyday English words such as ____________, lemon, ____________, and cotton arrived through Arabic trade and science.

lesson_6.watch_out: Do not think the Golden Age ended in the past without trace—its numerals, optics, hospital wards, and words remain part of daily life.
